opus-5.5.text:
I think benchmark saturation is real evidence, but it's weaker evidence than it first appears, and it's worth being careful about what it does and doesn't tell us.

The pattern over the last several years has been striking. A benchmark gets introduced, designed by smart people specifically to be hard for current systems, often with the expectation that it will last years. Then within a year or two, sometimes months, frontier models are near the ceiling. That has happened with reading comprehension, grade-school math, competition math, graduate-level science questions, and coding tasks. If you'd told people in 2018 that we'd see this, many would have taken it as a sign we were very close to general intelligence.

So I take it seriously. Each saturated benchmark rules out a particular story about what AI can't do. Every time someone says "models can't do X, that requires real understanding," and then they do X, that's a genuine update.

But there are a few reasons for caution.

First, benchmarks are by necessity things we can measure cleanly: questions with checkable answers, tasks that fit in a context window, problems with a well-defined endpoint. What makes humans economically and intellectually powerful is often the stuff that's hard to benchmark: sustained work over days or weeks, noticing which problem is worth solving, recovering from mistakes, operating in messy environments with unclear feedback. A benchmark can be saturated while the gap on those messier capabilities remains substantial.

Second, there's a selection and training effect. Once a benchmark becomes a target, labs optimise for it, sometimes directly, sometimes because similar data ends up in training. That doesn't make the progress fake, but it means a saturated score may overstate how well the capability generalises.

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting, the cost of reaching these scores matters. A lot of recent gains have come from scaling inference compute, letting models think much longer, sample many attempts, and so on. If you reach a high score by spending vastly more compute per task, that's a different kind of progress from a model that simply got smarter. It may still be enormously important, but it changes the economics and how quickly the capability spreads across the world.

The way I'd put it is that benchmark saturation tells you the frontier of narrow, well-specified cognitive tasks is moving very fast, faster than almost anyone predicted. What it doesn't directly tell you is how far we are from systems that can do the full range of things a capable human professional does autonomously. For that, I think the more informative measures are things like the length of task, in human time, that systems can reliably complete. That metric has also been growing quickly, which is concerning in its own way, but it gives you a better sense of the remaining distance than one more exam being aced.

So my overall view is that we should treat the saturation as a real signal that timelines could be short, and plan accordingly, while recognising that benchmarks systematically measure the parts of intelligence that are easiest to measure, and those may not be the last parts to fall.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark saturation does not directly tell us how far we are from systems that can perform the full range of work of a capable human professional, communicating that saturation alone does not show how many further advances are needed to reach AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we have to be quite careful about what benchmark saturation is actually telling us, because there are really two very different stories that fit the same observation, and people tend to slide between them.

The first story is the one you hear a lot: we built a test for some human capability, the models blew through it faster than anyone expected, so we must be closer to general intelligence than we thought. And there's something to that. If you'd told me ten years ago that systems would be getting these scores on graduate-level science questions or on competition mathematics, I would have taken it as strong evidence of something dramatic.

But the second story is that benchmarks are a somewhat strange instrument. They're designed by people who are trying to find things the current systems can't do, and when a benchmark saturates, that often tells us more about the benchmark than about the frontier of intelligence. There's a selection effect. Each benchmark gets built at the edge of what's currently possible, so by construction it's the kind of thing that's about to fall. And then once it falls, we're not left with a clean measurement of how far we've come; we're left needing a new ruler. So the sequence of saturations looks like exponential progress partly because we keep swapping in rulers calibrated to the last gap.

What I'd want to distinguish is the capability the benchmark is nominally about from the capability it actually tests. A lot of these evaluations are short, self-contained, well-specified problems where all the needed information is in front of you. That's a real skill, and humans find it hard, but it's a narrow slice of what we mean by being able to do intellectual work. The things that remain strikingly difficult are longer horizons: holding onto a goal over days, noticing when the problem you were given was the wrong problem, dealing with the fact that the world doesn't hand you the relevant context. The benchmarks that try to capture that, the ones that look at how long a task a system can complete reliably, are the ones I find more informative, and interestingly they show steady progress but not the sudden collapses you see elsewhere.

So my honest interpretation is something like this. Saturation is weak-to-moderate evidence that we're closer than the naive view held, because it keeps happening across quite different domains, and that's not nothing. But it's quite weak evidence about the precise distance, because the metric is partly measuring our own forecasting failures rather than the territory. If I wanted to know how close we are, I'd put more weight on the shape of the capability over time, the length and messiness of tasks systems can handle autonomously, than on the number of tests they've passed. And I'd hold the whole thing with some humility, because the one thing the last few years have reliably taught us is that our instruments for this are not very good.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark saturation is weak evidence about the precise distance to AGI and that successive saturations do not provide a clean measure of progress, communicating that they cannot show how many further benchmark advances are needed.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that we’re making substantial progress, but it’s quite difficult to translate that into a distance from AGI. A benchmark gives you a particular target, and when systems start doing very well on it, that tells you something real. But it doesn’t necessarily tell you how much of the space of intellectual tasks remains beyond them.

There’s a temptation to picture a kind of progress bar: we’ve passed these benchmarks, so perhaps we’re 80% of the way there. But we don’t have a well-defined denominator. We don’t know whether the remaining difficulties are things that will fall with another increment of the same techniques, or whether some will require substantial new ideas.

I’d also distinguish success on a test from being able to do the corresponding work reliably in the world. Answering a well-specified question is different from working out which question needs answering, pursuing it over a long period, and noticing when you’ve made a mistake.

So I would update towards taking shorter timelines more seriously, particularly when a system succeeds across quite different domains. But I wouldn’t infer a particular arrival date from benchmark saturation. It’s a reason to be less confident that AGI is far away, rather than a precise measure of how close it is.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance is difficult to translate into distance from AGI, that there is no well-defined denominator, and that it is unclear whether remaining difficulties will fall with another increment of current techniques. This communicates that benchmark saturation does not show how many further advances are needed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence that we’re making substantial progress, but it’s quite difficult to translate that into a distance from AGI. A benchmark gives us a kind of measuring stick, and then the system reaches the end of the stick. That tells us something real, but it doesn’t tell us how much further there is to go.

One concern is that we select benchmarks because they’re things we know how to measure. They may leave out capabilities that are essential for general intelligence, or test them in a rather artificial setting. And once a benchmark becomes a target, there’s a lot of effort directed towards doing well on it. So we should distinguish progress on the particular test from progress on the underlying ability we care about.

But I wouldn’t dismiss the pattern, either. If systems keep succeeding at tasks that we previously thought would require quite sophisticated intelligence, including new tasks designed after earlier benchmarks were saturated, that should update us towards taking further progress seriously.

What I’d resist is treating the proportion of benchmarks that have been solved as the proportion of the journey to AGI that we’ve completed. We don’t have a well-defined denominator. I’d be more interested in whether the systems can reliably generalise to unfamiliar problems, learn new things, and carry out extended tasks without someone continually steering them. Benchmark saturation is part of that evidence, rather than a clock counting down to AGI.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark saturation does not show how much further there is to go toward AGI and rejects treating solved benchmarks as a measure of the journey completed.
